unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7: Nature’s Power! In this unit, you will explore the incredible and sometimes dangerous forces of the natural world. You will learn about natural disasters such as cyclones, earthquakes, floods, droughts, and volcanic eruptions. You will discover how communities in East Africa and around the world prepare for these events, respond when they strike, and rebuild afterwards. Along the way, you will build a strong set of vocabulary words related to planning, science, government, and community action. You will also study an important grammar topic — how to use the Past Simple and Past Continuous tenses together, joined by connecting words like while, when, and until — to describe events that happened at the same time in the past. These skills will help you write powerful safety broadcasts, disaster reports, and opinion pieces about how people can work together when nature shows its strength.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the Vocabulary file and learn a few words from each group every day. Work through the five grammar mini-lessons, one or two at a time. Read the two texts, “When Nature Speaks” and “The Speech Under the Baobab”, and answer the comprehension questions. Then follow the main lesson in order: Key Vocabulary, Reading, Understanding the Text, Grammar Focus, Grammar Practice, Writing Workshop, Listening and Speaking, and Activities. Finish with the Check Your Learning self-assessment and the unit quiz.

readings.title: When Nature Speaks
readings.setting: Coastal and village communities facing natural events
readings.passageScript:
Last March, the weather changed quickly along the east coast of Africa. Dark clouds gathered above the Indian Ocean, and the wind grew stronger every hour. The local administration issued a declaration: a powerful cyclone was heading towards the coastal town of Mabari.
The preparation began at once. Families moved inland. Fishermen pulled their boats far up the beach. The school was converted into a shelter, a quick conversion that saved many lives. A large congregation of neighbours gathered in the town hall to hear the safety plan.
"We were watching the sky when the radio announcement came," said twelve-year-old Daniel. "My mother was cooking dinner, and my father was mending our fence. Everything stopped."
While the adults were loading supplies into lorries, the children helped carry water bottles and blankets. The distribution of food and clean water was organised by volunteers who worked through the night. They knew that fair distribution could save lives.
The cyclone arrived before dawn. Rain hammered the rooftops while the wind was howling like a wild animal. Trees bent and snapped. The sea pushed inland, flooding streets and farms. In one hour, the water level rose by more than a metre.
By morning, the wind had died down, but the damage was clear. Houses were broken. Crops were destroyed. Roads were covered in mud and fallen branches. Scientists later explained that heat conduction from the warm ocean surface had fed energy into the storm. When the warm, moist air rose high into the stratosphere, it created the spinning winds that made the cyclone so powerful.
"We knew the storm was coming because of modern mechanisation," explained a local teacher. "Weather stations and satellite images gave the administration enough time to act. Without that technology, many more people could have been hurt."
After the storm, restoration work began. Allies from neighbouring towns sent building materials and medicine. Engineers used careful calculation to check which roads and bridges were safe. An excavation team cleared mud from the school so that children could return to class.
The town held a public meeting. One elder made a declaration: "Nature has great power. We cannot stop a cyclone, but we can prepare, and we can rebuild." His words were a clear expression of the community's commitment to recovery.
Students from Mabari's school created illustrations showing the water cycle and how cyclones form. They wrote captions explaining each stage, and their teacher displayed the work on the notice board as a representation of what the children had learned.
Daniel added his own drawing: a picture of neighbours carrying sandbags side by side. Underneath, he wrote, "Preparation saves lives. Restoration rebuilds hope."
The experience taught everyone in Mabari that nature's power is real and enormous. Earthquakes shake the ground beneath our feet. Volcanoes send ash into the sky. Droughts dry the rivers for months. Floods sweep away everything in their path. But when communities work together, sharing resources, arranging fair distribution of supplies, and keeping a strong commitment to one another, they can face even the fiercest storm.
Nature speaks loudly. The question is whether we listen, prepare, and stand together when it does.

readings.title: The Speech Under the Baobab, part 1
readings.setting: Coastal and village communities facing natural events
readings.passageScript:
It was the dry season in Mbuma, and the dust hung low over the hills like a memory refusing to settle. A small congregation of villagers gathered beneath the baobab tree in the central square. Children whispered. Elders shifted their weight. Something important was coming.
Twelve-year-old Amal stood beside her grandfather, holding a folded sheet of paper in her hand. The administration had announced that students could now attend the weekly community forum, and Amal's school had chosen her to represent them.
"You will speak on behalf of the youth," Teacher Yasmin said. "It is called representation."
Amal's hands trembled, because her voice had never been heard by more than a classroom. Her grandfather placed a calm hand on her shoulder. "Speak the truth. Speak clearly. The baobab remembers."
Just days earlier, a big event had taken place in Mbuma. The local leader had made a public declaration that the economy would change. The country was leaving a capitalist model and adopting socialism, a system that promised fair distribution of wealth and public resources.
"We must shift towards equality," the leader had said. "Let us restore balance after years of unfair trade."
Many villagers had clapped, but others were worried. "What does socialism really mean?" someone had asked. "Will the shops close?" another whispered. "Could it cause inflation?" muttered Omar, a merchant. "My prices will have to rise."
Even Amal's parents were unsure. "Before, we had capitalism, with competition, ownership and private markets," her mother said. "Now they say we must share everything. It sounds better, but it worries me." "Systems are not just words," her father added. "They need care, not only promises."
The school had held a lesson on different systems. "Our current situation," said Teacher Yasmin, "comes from a capitalist model. But others include communism, where all resources are owned equally, and socialism, where things are shared fairly by law."
One boy raised his hand. "Which is better?" "That depends," the teacher replied. "Each system has its values and its failures." She drew three illustrations on the board: a market with coins, a factory with one large owner, and a shared field with many hands.
"Your task," she said, "is to write about which system could best help our village." Amal's group chose to write about restoration, about rebuilding after long hardship. They added a caption that said, "Shared power grows deep roots."
On forum day, Amal arrived early. Her classmate Sami joined her, carrying a chart with calculations that showed how food could be shared more fairly. "We used real data," he said. "With better distribution, we could feed forty more families every week."
Amal nodded. "But ideas must be spoken. Let us make sure we are heard."

readings.title: The Speech Under the Baobab, part 2
readings.setting: Coastal and village communities facing natural events
readings.passageScript:
The forum began with the head of the administration, who wore a beige suit and dark sunglasses.
"Citizens," he began, "we have started an initiative for change. This includes new trade agreements, updated copyright protections for local artists, and the expansion of modern farming machines, also known as mechanisation."
Amal listened carefully and scribbled notes: copyright means protecting ideas; mechanisation means machines that help farms. "But who benefits?" whispered Sami. "He did not say."
Then came the floor for community voices. An elder stood up. "I have farmed for forty years, and I do not understand these changes. Last week I tried to sell cassava and was told I needed a permit. My son says it is part of the new conversion system. What is that?"
The official responded, "We are converting from open selling to registered trade. It ensures fairer taxes." "But we are losing our freedom," the elder said, and the official looked away.
Next, a young woman spoke. "The new school fees are too high. I had to leave my studies because I could not afford them." A soft murmur spread through the crowd.
Then Omar the merchant spoke, sharp and direct. "The new system has potential, yes, but it also creates confusion. We used to know the rules. Now we are guessing." "It is a time of preparation," replied the official. "Change takes effort."
Finally, the moderator turned to the student speaker. "We welcome Amal." She stepped forward and felt the weight of every eye in the square.
"My name is Amal. I come as part of a new generation, but I speak with an old voice." She opened her folded paper. "While some were talking, others were planting. While systems changed, people still needed to eat. While the declaration was made, some children missed school."
The crowd was quiet. "We have studied capitalism, socialism, and communism. Each system speaks of justice, but justice is not automatic. It must be lived." She looked at the official. "You say there will be restoration. But we also ask: who decides what is restored? Who speaks for the ones without a microphone?"
Sami held up the chart. "With better calculation and careful distribution, no one needs to go hungry. The students have created models, and we ask that you review them."
There was a pause. Then a boy in the front row called out, "Go, Amal!" A few claps followed, then more. The official adjusted his tie. "We are revising our plans," he said slowly. "Perhaps we could meet the students next week."
After the forum, Amal sat beneath the baobab tree. "You did well," her grandfather said. "I spoke with my true expression," she replied. "And the baobab remembers," he said, smiling.

readings.title: The Speech Under the Baobab, part 3
readings.setting: Coastal and village communities facing natural events
readings.passageScript:
Later that month, new proposals were posted on the school notice board. The initiative would now include a council of student and teacher representatives, a review of the calculation methods used for food sharing, a declaration of student voices in community meetings, and a pilot programme for pollinator gardens and local pollination studies.
Amal's class created illustrations and wrote captions for each proposal. Sami added a note: "Representation is more than attendance. It is presence." The administration even added a line of its own: "Thanks to the students' commitment, the system grows stronger."
That weekend, a guest visited their classroom, a researcher from the city. "I have read your work," she told them. "I am preparing a historical excavation of local economies, and you have made a real impact."
"We are only twelve," said Sami, blinking. "Age does not limit insight," she replied, "just as systems do not limit dreams."
Amal raised her hand. "Could we write our own script? Something like a declaration of values for the next generation." The researcher nodded. "With your permission, I will even help you share it."
That evening, Amal walked home under a wide sky. She thought about allies and preparation, about restoration and hope, and about how a single clear voice could help a whole community stand together.

readings.title: Voices After the Storm
readings.setting: Coastal and village communities facing natural events
readings.passageScript:
Two short accounts help us understand what people feel when nature shows its power. Read them slowly, and notice how each speaker uses time words to order the events.
A Survivor Remembers.
"My name is Maya, and I am thirteen years old. I live in a small fishing village on the coast. Last year, a terrible cyclone hit our area. I was studying for my exams when the wind started to scream. My mother was preparing dinner while my little brother was playing outside. We heard the warning on the radio and ran to the school shelter. We waited there until the storm finally passed. The next morning our house was damaged, but we were all safe. The whole congregation of the village helped each other. People shared food, and allies from the next town brought medicine and clean water. I learned that careful preparation really does save lives."
A Nature Report.
Today, scientists confirmed that the earthquake measured 5.2 on the scale used to record ground movement. While people were going about their normal day, the ground began to shake at exactly two o'clock in the afternoon. Buildings trembled and glass fell from windows. The administration issued a declaration within minutes, telling everyone to move to open spaces away from tall walls. Volunteers began a careful excavation of one collapsed building. When the rescuers arrived, they found all fifteen people inside safe and alive. The restoration of the damaged roads will begin next week, and engineers are already using calculation to decide which bridges are strong enough to reopen.
Both speakers remind us that nature is powerful, but that preparation, fair distribution of help, and loyal allies can carry a community through the hardest days.

grammar.title: Past Simple vs Past Continuous
grammar.explanation: The Past Simple describes actions that are finished. The Past Continuous describes actions that were happening — still in progress — at a certain moment in the past. When we use them together, we can tell vivid stories about events that happened at the same time or interrupted each other. This is especially useful when describing natural disasters, emergencies, or any event where many things were happening at once.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
How to form it:
Past Simple:
Regular verbs: add -ed → walk → walked, prepare → prepared.
Irregular verbs: learn special forms → go → went, see → saw, break → broke, send → sent.
Past Continuous:
I / he / she / it + was + verb-ing: “She was cooking dinner.”
you / we / they + were + verb-ing: “They were running to the shelter.”
Combined pattern: Past Continuous (background action) + when + Past Simple (interruption).
“I was reading when the earthquake struck.”
“They were sleeping when the alarm went off.”
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often drop the helper verb and write "They playing football when it rained." The Past Continuous always needs was or were before the -ing verb.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture the Past Continuous as a video that is still playing, and the Past Simple as the photograph snapped in the middle of it.
grammar.practice:
Part A: fill each gap with the Past Simple or Past Continuous. 1. I ___ (watch) the news when the earthquake ___ (hit). 2. While they ___ (build) the shelter, the rain ___ (start). 3. She ___ (walk) to school when she ___ (hear) the siren.
Part B: continue. 4. The volunteers ___ (distribute) food when more supplies ___ (arrive). 5. We ___ (study) in class while the wind ___ (blow) outside.
Part C: write two sentences of your own about a storm, each pairing one Past Continuous action with one Past Simple interruption.

===
Answer Key (self-check — read this only after you finish Parts A and B):
Part A: 1. I was watching the news when the earthquake hit. 2. While they were building the shelter, the rain started. 3. She was walking to school when she heard the siren.
Part B: 4. The volunteers were distributing food when more supplies arrived. 5. We were studying in the classroom while the wind was blowing outside.
Part C (open-ended — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): Model example to compare your work against: "We were sitting on the porch when the thunder rumbled. The dog was barking loudly until the rain finally stopped."

grammar.title: Connecting Words for Time (while, when, until)
grammar.explanation: Connecting words for time — also called time conjunctions — help us show how two events relate to each other in time. Using them correctly makes our stories clearer and our writing more interesting.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
How to form and use it:
while — two actions happening at the same time:
“I listened to the radio while I studied.”
“While the wind was blowing, trees fell to the ground.”
when — a specific moment, often an interruption:
“I was sleeping when the alarm rang.”
“When the flood came, the village was not ready.”
until — something continues up to a point and then stops:
“We waited until the storm passed.”
“The volunteers worked until every family had food.”
You may also use after (something that happens later) and before (something that happens earlier):
“After the earthquake, the community began to rebuild.”
“Before the storm arrived, the families moved inland.”
grammar.commonMistake: Writers often choose while for a sudden event, as in "I was sleeping while the alarm rang." A short, interrupting action needs when, not while.
grammar.memoryTip: While means two things at once, when means one exact moment, and until means right up to a stopping point.

===
Answer Key (self-check — read this only after you finish Parts A and B):
Part A: 1. While the storm was approaching, the radio played warnings. 2. I was eating breakfast when the ground began to shake. 3. We stayed in the shelter until the rescue team arrived.
Part B: 4. While the adults were clearing the roads, the children carried water. 5. The fishermen did not sail until the waves calmed down.

grammar.title: Imperatives for Giving Instructions
grammar.explanation: Imperatives are command words that tell someone what to do. They are very important during emergencies and natural disasters, when instructions must be clear, short, and direct. For example: “Move to higher ground.” “Do not walk through floodwater.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
How to form it:
Start with the base form of the verb (no subject needed): “Prepare your emergency bag.”
Add “Do not” or “Don’t” for a negative command: “Do not go near the river.”
Add “Please” for a polite command: “Please stay inside until the wind stops.”
You can use “Let’s” to include yourself: “Let’s work together to clear the road.”
grammar.commonMistake: Some learners add a subject and write "You prepare your bag." An imperative starts straight from the base verb, as in "Prepare your bag."
grammar.memoryTip: Think of an imperative as your emergency voice: short, calm, and starting with the action word, with no time for a subject.

Part B: 4. Prepare food for three days. 5. Stay calm.
Part C (open-ended — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): Model example to compare your work against: "Flood Safety Notice. Please move to higher ground immediately. Do not walk through moving floodwater. Take your emergency bag with you. Stay calm and listen for further instructions."

grammar.title: Adjectives + Prepositions for Feelings
grammar.explanation: In English, we often describe our feelings using an adjective followed by a preposition. This helps us say exactly what we feel and what caused the feeling. For example: “I am amazed by the restoration.” “She is interested in how cyclones form.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
How to form it:
Subject + be + adjective + preposition + object.
amazed by: “We were amazed by the power of the storm.”
interested in: “He is interested in studying natural disasters.”
worried about: “The farmers were worried about the drought.”
proud of: “The community is proud of its commitment to rebuilding.”
surprised by: “I was surprised by how quickly the allies arrived.”
excited about: “The students were excited about presenting their illustrations.”
scared of: “Some children were scared of the thunder.”
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to pick the wrong preposition, as in "I am interested by science." The fixed pair is interested in, so learn each adjective with its own partner.
grammar.memoryTip: Store each pair as one chunk on a flashcard, such as amazed by, worried about and proud of, and say the two words together every time.
grammar.practice:

Part B: continue. 4. The town is proud ___ its community spirit. 5. They were surprised ___ how much damage the flood caused.

Part A: 1. amazed by 2. worried about 3. interested in
Part B: 4. proud of 5. surprised by
Part C (open-ended — this is your own writing, so there is no single fixed answer): Model example to compare your work against: "The villagers were amazed by how quickly the water rose. They were worried about their crops. Afterwards, everyone was proud of how the community worked together."

grammar.title: Could + Verb (Possibility)
grammar.explanation: The modal verb could helps us talk about things that are possible but not certain. This is useful when we discuss what might happen during or after a natural disaster, or when we suggest ideas. For example: “This could cause serious flooding.” “Allies could send food and medicine.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
How to form it:
Subject + could + base form of the verb (no -s, no -ing, no -ed).
“The drought could last for several more months.”
“This policy could improve the distribution of food.”
“It could cause inflation if supplies run out.”
“Could we write our own script?” (from the story)
grammar.commonMistake: Learners sometimes add to after could, writing "She could to leave." After could, use the plain base verb with no to, as in "She could leave."
grammar.memoryTip: Imagine could as a door standing open: the action is possible, but nobody has walked through it yet.

Part A: 1. The rising river could flood the farmland. 2. This plan could save many lives. 3. The earthquake could damage older buildings.

grammar.title: Building a Vivid Past-Tense Paragraph
grammar.explanation: Strong Grade 6 writers combine the Past Simple, the Past Continuous and the connecting words while, when and until so that a whole paragraph reads as one clear sequence of events.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Set the scene with a Past Continuous action, then interrupt it with a Past Simple event, and use while, when or until to join them. For example: "The volunteers were loading the lorries when the second wave struck, and they kept working until every family was safe." Read the finished paragraph aloud and check that each joined pair of actions makes sense in time.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers often switch tenses without a reason, mixing was working and worked in the same clause. Decide whether each action is a background action or a completed event before you choose the tense.
grammar.memoryTip: Background first, event second: start with the video that is still playing, then drop in the photograph.

Dear members of the administration,
I am writing on behalf of the students to ask you to review our food-sharing plan. When we first calculated the amounts for each family, we noticed that the distribution was uneven, and some households received too little while others received too much.

Yours sincerely,
Sami

writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short information text explaining how a cyclone forms and why it is so powerful. Use the science from the reading, including conduction from the warm ocean and warm air rising into the stratosphere. writing.modelText:
How a Cyclone Forms
A cyclone begins over a warm ocean, where the sea heats the air above it through conduction. As the warm, moist air rises quickly, it cools and forms thick clouds, and more air rushes in to take its place, spinning the whole system faster.
High above, the rising air reaches the stratosphere and spreads outward like a giant umbrella. This constant movement pulls in more warm, moist air from the ocean below, which is why a cyclone can grow so powerful before it reaches the coast.
